source_text: Οὕτω δὲ εἶπε δεικνὺς, ὅτι δικαίως ἔμελλεν ἀλγεῖν ἐπὶ τῇ τελευτῇ τοῦ μαθητοῦ. Καὶ τὴν ἀρετὴν δὲ αὐτοῦ πάλιν ἐκκαλύπτει πᾶσιν, οὑτωσὶ λέγων, ὅτι Ἤγγισε μέχρι θανάτου παραβουλευσάμενος τῇ ψυχῇ, ἵνα ἀναπληρώσῃ τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα τῆς πρός με λειτουργίας. Τί γένοιτ' ἂν ἐκείνων μακαριώτερον, τί δὲ ἡμῶν ἀθλιώτερον; εἴ γε ἐκεῖνοι μὲν καὶ τὸ αἷμα, καὶ τὴν ψυχὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν διδασκάλων προΐεντο, ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐδὲ ῥῆμα ψιλὸν πολλάκις προέσθαι τολμῶμεν ὑπὲρ τῶν κοινῶν πατέρων, ἀλλὰ ἀκούοντες αὐτοὺς βλασφημουμένους, λοιδορουμένους κακῶς καὶ παρὰ τῶν οἰκείων καὶ παρὰ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων, οὐκ ἐπιστομίζομεν τοὺς λέγοντας, οὐ κωλύομεν, οὐκ ἐλέγχομεν. Εἴθε μὲν οὖν μὴ αὐτοὶ τῆς κακηγορίας ἤρχομεν ταύτης. Νυνὶ δὲ οὐ τοσαῦτα παρὰ τῶν ἀπίστων σκώμματα καὶ ὀνείδη, ὅσα παρὰ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναι πιστῶν καὶ μεθ' ἡμῶν τετάχθαι γινόμενα εἰς τοὺς ἄρχοντας ἴδοι τις ἄν. Ἔτι οὖν ζητήσομεν πόθεν ῥᾳθυμία τοσαύτη καὶ εὐλαβείας ὑπεροψία γέγονεν, ὅταν οὕτως ὦμεν ἀπεχθῶς πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας διακείμενοι τοὺς ἡμετέρους; Οὐ γάρ ἐστιν, οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲν, ὃ καταλῦσαι καὶ διαφθεῖραι Ἐκκλησίαν δύναιτ' ἂν, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐκ ἔστιν οὕτω γενέσθαι τοῦτο ἀλλαχόθεν ῥᾳδίως, ἀλλ' ἢ ὅταν οἱ μαθηταὶ τοῖς διδασκάλοις, καὶ τοῖς πατράσιν οἱ παῖδες, καὶ τοῖς ἄρχουσιν οἱ ἀρχόμενοι μὴ μετὰ πολλῆς ὦσι συνδεδεμένοι τῆς ἀκριβείας. Εἶτα ἂν μὲν τὸν ἀδελφόν τις εἴπῃ κακῶς, καὶ τῆς ἀναγνώσεως τῶν θείων ἀπείργεται Γραφῶν. Ἵνα τί γὰρ ἀναλαμβάνεις τὴν διαθήκην μου διὰ στόματός σου; φησὶν ὁ Θεός· εἶτα τὴν αἰτίαν τιθεὶς, ἐπήγαγε· Καθήμενος κατὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου κατελάλεις. Τὸν πνευματικὸν δὲ πατέρα κατηγορῶν, ἄξιον εἶναι νομίζεις σαυτὸν ἐπιβῆναι τῶν ἱερῶν προθύρων; Καὶ πῶς ἂν ἔχοι λόγον; Εἰ γὰρ οἱ κακολογοῦντες πατέρα ἢ μητέρα θανάτῳ τελευτῶσι, ποίας ἄξιος ἔσται δίκης ὁ τὸν πολλῷ τῶν γονέων ἐκείνων ἀναγκαιότερον ὄντα καὶ βελτίω τολμῶν λέγειν κακῶς; Καὶ οὐ δέδοικε, μήποτε διαστᾶσα ἡ γῆ παντελῶς αὐτὸν ἀφανίσῃ, ἢ σκηπτὸς ἄνωθεν κατενεχθεὶς καταφλέξῃ τὴν κατήγορον γλῶτταν; Οὐκ ἤκουσας τί πέπονθεν ἡ Μωϋσέως ἀδελφὴ κατειποῦσα τοῦ ἄρχοντος; πῶς ἀκάθαρτος γέγονε, καὶ εἰς λέπραν ἐνέπεσε, καὶ τὴν ἐσχάτην ὑπέμεινεν ἀτιμίαν, καὶ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ παρακαλοῦντος καὶ τῷ Θεῷ προσπίπτοντος, οὐδεμιᾶς ἔτυχε συγγνώμης, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκθεμένη τὸν ἅγιον ἐκεῖνον, καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἀνατροφὴν αὐτοῦ συντελέσασα, καὶ ὅπως ἡ μήτηρ γένοιτο τροφὸς, καὶ μὴ ἐν βαρβαρικῇ χειρὶ τραφῇ τὸ παιδίον ἐξαρχῆς συμπράξασα, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα στρατηγήσασα τοῦ γυναικείου γένους, καθάπερ Μωϋσῆς τοῦ τῶν ἀνδρῶν, καὶ πάντα συνδιενεγκοῦσα τὰ δεινὰ, καὶ ἀδελφὴ Μωϋσέως οὖσα, οὐδὲν ὅμως ἀπὸ τούτων ἁπάντων ἐκέρδανεν εἰς τὸ διαφυγεῖν τὴν ὀργὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ κακηγορίᾳ; ἀλλ' ὁ Μωϋσῆς, ὁ τοσοῦτον λαὸν ἐξαιτησάμενος μετὰ τὴν ἄφατον ἀσέβειαν ἐκείνην, οὗτος ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀδελφῆς προσπίπτων καὶ συγγνώμην αἰτῶν, οὐκ ἴσχυσεν ἵλεω ποιῆσαι τὸν Θεὸν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπετιμᾶτο σφοδρῶς· ἵνα μάθωμεν ἡμεῖς ὅσον κακόν ἐστι, τὸ τοὺς ἄρχοντας λέγειν κακῶς, καὶ τοὺς ἑτέρων κρίνειν βίους. Καὶ γὰρ ἐπὶ τῆς ἡμέρας ἐκείνης, οὐκ ἀφ' ὧν ἁμαρτάνομεν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀφ' ὧν ἑτέροις ἐψηφισάμεθα, κρινεῖ πάντως ἡμῖν ὁ Θεός· καὶ πολλάκις ὃ τῇ φύσει κοῦφόν ἐστιν ἁμάρτημα, τοῦτο χαλεπὸν καὶ ἀσύγγνωστον γίγνεται τῇ τοῦ ἁμαρτάνοντος περὶ ἑτέρου κρίσει.
thought_title: The danger of slandering spiritual fathers
orientation: Chrysostom is contrasting the devotion of Paul's disciples with his own hearers' failure to defend their spiritual fathers, and now warns of the judgment on those who slander them.
pass_a_gloss: Thus he spoke, showing that he was justly about to grieve at the death of the disciple. And again he reveals his virtue to all, saying thus: that he drew near to death, having risked his life, in order that he might fill up your lack of service toward me. What could be more blessed than those men, and what more wretched than us? If indeed those men gave both blood and life on behalf of their teachers, but we do not dare to give even a bare word often on behalf of our common fathers, but hearing them blasphemed, reviled wickedly both by their own people and by strangers, we do not silence those who speak, we do not hinder, we do not refute. Would that we did not ourselves begin this slander. But as it is, one would see not so many mockeries and reproaches from the unfaithful as are done against the rulers by those who seem to be faithful and to have been ranked with us. Shall we still seek whence so great carelessness and contempt of piety has come, when we are so hostilely disposed toward our own fathers? For there is not, there is not anything which could destroy and corrupt the Church, or rather it is not possible for this to happen easily from any other source, except when the disciples are not bound to the teachers, and the children to the fathers, and the subjects to the rulers with much exactness. Then if someone speaks evil of a brother, he is also barred from the reading of the divine Scriptures. For why do you take up my covenant in your mouth? says God; then adding the reason, he brought in: Sitting, you spoke against your brother. But accusing a spiritual father, do you consider yourself worthy to set foot on the sacred thresholds? And how would this have reason? For if those who speak evil of father or mother die by death, of what punishment will he be worthy who dares to speak evil of the one who is much more necessary and better than those parents? And does he not fear lest the earth splitting apart utterly destroy him, or a thunderbolt brought down from above burn up the accusing tongue? Did you not hear what the sister of Moses suffered when she spoke against the ruler? How she became unclean, and fell into leprosy, and endured the utmost dishonor, and though her brother entreated and fell before God, she obtained no pardon, but even having exposed that holy one, and having contributed to his upbringing, and having cooperated from the beginning so that the mother might become his nurse and the child might not be raised in a barbarian hand, and after these things having led the female race, just as Moses led the race of men, and having shared in all the dangers, and being the sister of Moses, she nevertheless gained nothing from all these things toward escaping the wrath of God for the slander? But Moses, who had interceded for so great a people after that unspeakable impiety, this man falling down on behalf of his sister and asking pardon, was not able to make God propitious, but was also rebuked severely; in order that we might learn how great an evil it is to speak evil of rulers and to judge the lives of others. For on that day, not only from the things we sin, but also from the things we have voted against others, God will certainly judge us; and often what is by nature a light sin, this becomes harsh and unpardonable through the sinner's judgment about another.

choices.why: The verb means to expose oneself to danger; τῇ ψυχῇ is a dative of respect, so 'having risked his life' captures the sense of endangering his own soul/life.

choices.term: τὸ ὑμῶν ὑστέρημα τῆς πρός με λειτουργίας
choices.english: your lack of service toward me
choices.why: ὑστέρημα means deficiency or lack; λειτουργία here is service rendered to Paul, so the phrase means the shortfall in what they could do for him directly.
rejected: your deficiency of ministry to me
what was lacking in your service to me

choices.why: ψιλός means bare or mere; the contrast is between giving blood and life versus even a simple spoken word in defense.
In context this refers to spiritual rulers, the clergy; 'rulers' preserves the source term and its force in Chrysostom's argument about authority.
ἀκάθαρτος is the standard term for ritual uncleanness, fitting the leprosy context of Miriam's punishment.
ἐκτίθημι means to expose or set out; this refers to Miriam's role in placing the infant Moses in the basket, so 'exposed' is the literal and historically apt rendering.
rejected: having set out that holy one
having laid out that holy one

bible_refs.note: Ἵνα τί γὰρ ἀναλαμβάνεις τὴν διαθήκην μου διὰ στόματός σου; ... Καθήμενος κατὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου κατελάλεις

pass_b_english: He said this to show that he would rightly grieve over the death of his disciple. And again he reveals his virtue to everyone, saying: "He came near to death, having disregarded his life, so that he might fill up your lack of service toward me." What could be more blessed than those people, and what more wretched than us? For they gave even their blood and their lives for their teachers, while we often do not dare to give even a bare word for our common fathers. When we hear them blasphemed and reviled, both by their own people and by strangers, we do not silence those who speak, we do not stop them, we do not rebuke them. If only we ourselves did not begin this slander! But as it is, one could see that not so many mockeries and insults come from unbelievers against the rulers as come from those who seem to be believers and are ranked among us. Will we still ask where such carelessness and contempt for reverence came from, when we are so hostilely disposed toward our own fathers? For there is nothing—nothing at all—that could destroy and ruin the Church, or rather, this cannot easily happen from any other source, except when disciples are not bound to their teachers, children to their fathers, and subjects to their rulers with great exactness. Then, if someone speaks evil of a brother, he is barred from the reading of the divine Scriptures. "Why do you take up my covenant in your mouth?" God says. Then, giving the reason, he added: "You sat and spoke against your brother" (Psalm 49:16, 20 LXX; Psalm 50:16, 20 Hebrew). But if you accuse your spiritual father, do you think yourself worthy to step onto the sacred threshold? How could that make sense? For if those who speak evil of father or mother die by death, what punishment will be worthy for the one who dares to speak evil of the one who is far more necessary and better than those parents? And does he not fear that the earth might split apart and utterly destroy him, or that a thunderbolt might come down from above and burn up his accusing tongue? Have you not heard what happened to the sister of Moses when she spoke against the ruler? How she became unclean and fell into leprosy, and endured the utmost dishonor? And though her brother pleaded and fell before God, she received no forgiveness. She had exposed that holy one as an infant, and had cooperated in his upbringing, and in arranging how the mother might become his nurse, so that the child would not be raised by a barbarian hand. And after that she led the women, just as Moses led the men, and shared in bearing all the dangers. And though she was the sister of Moses, she gained nothing from all these things to escape the wrath of God for her slander. But Moses, who had secured pardon for so great a people after that unspeakable impiety, fell down for his sister and asked for pardon, yet could not make God merciful. He was even rebuked severely—so that we might learn how great an evil it is to speak evil of rulers and to judge the lives of others. For on that day, God will judge us not only for the sins we have committed, but also for the judgments we have passed on others. And often a sin that is light by nature becomes grave and unpardonable through the sinner's judgment of another.

problems.quote: And though her brother pleaded and fell before God, she received no forgiveness.
problems.source_quote: καὶ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ παρακαλοῦντος καὶ τῷ Θεῷ προσπίπτοντος, οὐδεμιᾶς ἔτυχε συγγνώμης
problems.why: Missing: Moses fell before God too, not just pleaded; καὶ τῷ Θεῷ προσπίπτοντος is omitted.

problems.quote: She had exposed that holy one
problems.source_quote: ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκθεμένη τὸν ἅγιον ἐκεῖνον
problems.why: ἐκθεμένη means 'exposing' a child (abandonment), not 'exposing' in the sense of revealing. Miriam exposed baby Moses as an infant.
problems.fix: She had exposed that holy one as an infant
problems.ruling: ἐκθεμένη means 'exposed' (abandoned) infant Moses, not 'revealed' him; meaning changed.

dismissed.quote: she led the women, just as Moses led the men
dismissed.why: στρατηγέω means 'to be general/leader of,' not simply 'led.' The military term emphasizes command, not mere guidance.
dismissed.note: 'Led the women' is a fair, natural rendering of στρατηγήσασα; demanding 'general' is a stylistic preference.

dismissed.quote: exposed that holy one as an infant
dismissed.why: ἐκτίθημι means 'to expose' (leave out to die), but Miriam placed Moses in the Nile to save him, not to expose him to death. The English 'exposed' carries the wrong sense of abandonment.
dismissed.note: ἐκθεμένη literally means 'exposed' or 'set out', and the English keeps Chrysostom's own word; 'placed in the reeds' would add detail not in the source.
